title: Adaptation of Computer Use Agents to New Software with User Manuals
authors: Chulhoon Yoon, Kyungri Park, Jinyeong Yun et al.
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have significantly improved the ability to operate real-world software through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) using visual observations and natural language instructions. However, maintaining strong performance on unseen applications remains challenging, as practical tasks often require long-horizon procedural knowledge and application-specific operation patterns. title: NL2SQL with Iterative Self-Refinement
authors: Anjali Vemula, Akshat Dasula
abstract: Bridging the gap between human intent and machine logic remains a critical challenge in data access for non-technical users, yet Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable: they hallucinate schema elements, generate syntactically invalid queries, or fail to capture user intent. These limitations are especially critical in domains such as insurance, where KPIs, regulatory constraints, and legacy relational systems demand high precision. We introduce a multi-agent, persona-driven NL2SQL framew

title: Beyond Surface Cues: Robust LLM-Generated Korean Text Detection
authors: SungHo Kim, SangKeun Lee
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) generate increasingly fluent text, the need for reliable detection of LLM-generated content has grown substantially. However, existing research remains heavily English-centric, leaving Korean largely underexplored. Moreover, current evaluations of Korean text detection often rely on superficial cues, leading to overly optimistic estimates of detection performance. title: Multiple Turns, Short Horizons: Measuring Effective-Horizon Compression in Jailbreaks
authors: Zhipeng Wei, Michael Lee, N. Benjamin Erichson
abstract: Multi-turn jailbreaks use feedback from a victim large language model to adapt their queries over several turns. However, once an effective trajectory has been found, it is unclear how much of the earlier query history is still needed. In this work, we study this by removing early attacker queries and running the remaining queries again in a new conversation while regenerating the victim's responses. We define the effective horizon as the shortest remaining query sequence that recovers the same

title: Veil-Then-Reveal: Protecting PII Privacy via Reversible Pseudo-Anonymization in Zero-Trust User--LLM Interaction
authors: Mohamed Shaaban, Mohamed Elmahallawy, Thomas E. Carroll
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly process sensitive documents and personal information, yet sending prompts containing personally identifiable information (PII) to remote providers exposes data subjects and organizations to risks from logging, retention, model training, and unintended disclosure. Existing anonymization methods often mask or remove PII, while conventional encryption eliminates the lexical and structural cues needed for effective LLM processing. We present Veil-then-Reveal

title: Prune the Leaky Neurons: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in Fine-Tuned LLMs via Joint-Embedding-Guided Pruning
authors: Mohamed Shaaban, Mohamed Elmahallawy
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on proprietary records enables domain adaptation but introduces two challenges: (i) privacy leakage of memorized private data, such as personally identifiable information (PII), and (ii) balancing private data removal with utility preservation. Existing defenses, including data sanitization and differential privacy, often degrade performance, while privacy-neuron editing lacks a PII-free reference to distinguish identity-specific neurons from those suppor

title: FuTransformer: FP8 prefill and INT4 decode for Llama-style inference on Hopper
authors: Wei Wang
abstract: Transformer prefill reuses weights across tokens and is dominated by matrix multiplication and activation data movement; single-token decode has limited reuse and is dominated by weight and KV-cache reads. We present FUTRANSFORMER, a CUDA implementation of a Llama-style Transformer block for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. title: Steering beyond Language: Improving Multilingual Training-Free Text Embeddings via Paired-Residual Subspace Removal
authors: Ailiang Lin, Zhuoyun Li, Yusong Wang et al.
abstract: While deriving text embeddings directly from frozen LLMs has emerged as a promising direction, existing methods focus almost exclusively on English, leaving multilingual settings largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of multilingual training-free text embeddings in LLMs. Our analysis reveals a language-conditioned embedding geometry in which semantically equivalent sentences remain misaligned across languages. We hypothesize that language-specific variation can

title: Out of Support, Not Out of Reach: In-Context Learning with Unsupported Instructions and Composed Tasks
authors: Xuhan Tong, Yuchen Zeng, Jiawei Zhang
abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) enables pretrained LLMs to adapt to downstream tasks from a small set of input-output demonstrations, without parameter updates. Yet existing theory primarily explains ICL as identifying a latent task already represented in pretraining, leaving unclear whether ICL can succeed when either the instruction or the target task falls outside the pretraining support. We develop a theoretical framework under mild assumptions that separates these two forms of distribution shift.

title: Predictable Scaling: Efficient Model Exploration via Scaling-Law Prediction
authors: Aishwarya Wesanekar, Sheng-Tao Yang, Jiawei Zhang et al.
abstract: Evaluating candidate changes (hypotheses) to recommendation models requires full-scale training runs consuming thousands of GPU-hours, severely limiting the hypothesis space engineers can feasibly explore. We introduce Predictable Scaling (PS), a systematic framework that exploits empirically verified regularity conditions to predict full-scale model performance from small-scale proxies. PS constructs scaled-down variants via composable scaling functions along distinct resource axes, and project

title: Generative Policy Improvement from Observational Data
authors: Jonas Schweisthal, Dennis Frauen, Stefan Feuerriegel et al.
abstract: We study how to improve decision policies from observational data to generate better actions when actions are complex, structured objects, such as text messages or images. This task is subject to two major challenges: (i) action-level overlap is often too weak for reliable off-policy evaluation and improvement, and (ii) generating new structured actions often requires expensive training or fine-tuning (e.g., of an LLM) and can be ill-defined due to information loss in action representations. To

title: Minimax-optimal Scaling Laws in Ridge Regression via Transfer Learning
authors: Yalda Shabanzadeh, Diyuan Wu, Marco Mondelli
abstract: Pretrained models are often reused across downstream tasks, motivating the question of whether this transfer learning procedure can provide a substantial performance improvement, namely, in terms of the scaling law. We address this question in the prototypical setting of high-dimensional regression, where (i) a pretrained \emph{source} model is trained via ridge regression, and (ii) a fine-tuned \emph{target} model is regularized via the $L_2$ distance from the source estimator. First, we establ

title: Sample, Mix, or Verify? Allocating Test-Time Compute under Imperfect Verifiers
authors: Srinivasan Iyengar
abstract: A common way to make language models and agents more accurate is to spend more compute at inference time: generate many candidate solutions and submit the one a verifier prefers. Success then requires that some candidate is correct and that the verifier picks it. The first grows predictably with the number of samples; the second does not, because real verifiers (unit tests, majority votes, LLM judges, reward models) accept wrong answers, reject right ones, and make correlated mistakes. title: Process Reward Modeling with Reliability- and Conservatism-Aware Bayesian Belief
authors: Zhongjian Qiao, Zhixiang Zhou, Jiafei Lyu et al.
abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) play a central role in test-time scaling for large language model (LLM) reasoning. However, PRMs may provide inaccurate process rewards for test-time scaling, which we identify as arising from two sources of uncertainty: (1) \textit{PRM uncertainty} that arises from insufficient supervision data and imperfect PRM training; and (2) \textit{policy uncertainty} that results from the mismatch between the policy to collect supervision data and the policy for test-time sca

title: A Stronger Teacher Within: Strengthening MoE Models via On-Policy Bidirectional Distillation
authors: Haoyu Chen, Jun Bai, Yang Liu et al.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, but its outcome-level rewards provide only sparse supervision. On-Policy Distillation offers dense token-level feedback, yet requires a stronger compatible teacher, while on-policy self-distillation relies on hand-designed privileged information. title: WebCoder: Scaling General Frontend Development with Artifact-Grounded Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zijun Dou, Zhen Yang, Xijun Liu et al.
abstract: Real-world frontend development requires agents to compose reproduction, generation, modification, and repair over an evolving application state. Learning a general policy for this process requires translating heterogeneous execution feedback into task-aligned rewards and effective credit assignment across long sequences of interdependent actions. We introduce WebCoder, a general frontend development agent trained with artifact-grounded agentic reinforcement learning. Our key idea is to assess d

title: ShadowFPT: Backdooring Federated Prompt Tuning via Shadow Triggers
authors: Kun Zhai, Teng Li, Yunhao Feng et al.
abstract: Federated Prompt Tuning (FPT) adapts large vision--language models by freezing the pretrained backbone and optimizing only lightweight prompt parameters across clients. Although this design improves communication and parameter efficiency, it creates an overlooked security risk. Since the backbone is shared and frozen, a malicious client can induce backdoor behavior through the representation space while keeping its uploaded prompt updates close to benign ones. title: Benchmarking and Enhancing Agentic Causal Discovery
authors: Pingchuan Ma, Rui Ding, Shuai Wang
abstract: LLM agents can now run causal discovery algorithms on a dataset and report what comes out. Whether they do more than that, such as noticing where an algorithm went wrong and fixing it with further tests, is hard to tell from current benchmarks. Most of them give the variables meaningful names, and an LLM shown only the names of the Tübingen cause-effect pairs already gets 99% of the directions right. title: VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations Research
authors: Minbo Ma, Honglin Zhang, Bangtao Zhou et al.
abstract: Advances in reasoning, coding, and tool use enable LLM agents to solve operations research (OR) problems through iterative problem modeling, program construction, and verification. Yet passing self-authored verification does not ensure that the solutions satisfy task constraints and meet optimization quality. This gap can arise from correlated specification errors, where the generated program and its checks share omissions or misinterpretations of task requirements, alongside incomplete verifica

title: Unbounded Losses, Unchecked Inputs: Measuring the Safeguards of LLM Options-Trading Agents
authors: Mengxiao Wang, Nitesh Saxena
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now place options orders at retail brokers, and developers publish open-source options agents faster than anyone has examined them. Prior security work on trading agents scored academic equities designs by whether an attacker can flip a buy-or-sell decision. We present the first measurement of the options agents that brokers and developers ship, scored by the safeguards they enforce and by the worst loss their documented order paths can reach. title: Cortex: A Fixed-Point Theory of Governed Coding Agents - Technical Report
authors: Marius-Constantin Dinu, Florian Zeba
abstract: A coding agent combines a large language model (LLM) with a harness that plans, edits, and executes code. We study Cortex, a supervisory layer for pre-execution governance, requirement tracking, and iterative validation and repair. We formalize requirement closure on a finite lattice. title: Who Plans, Who Edits? Verified, Cost-Aware Division of Labor for LLM-Driven Analog Layout Repair
authors: Xilai Dai, Saeed Mohammadi
abstract: Language-model agents can repair analog layouts when sign-off tools check every edit, but which model should plan a repair, which should edit it, and at what cost remain open questions. In our tool-grounded repair agent, models only choose bounded layout operators; sign-off tools rerun each task's contract checks after every edit, so failing layouts are never accepted. title: LoopHIL: Looping Hardware into LLM-assisted Agents for Wireless Embedded Systems
authors: Dhairya Shah, Spanddhana Sara, Savitha Viswanadh Kandala et al.
abstract: LLM agents are widely used for software development and debugging, but their adoption in embedded systems, especially for wireless tasks, remains limited. This is because embedded development requires hardware-in-the-loop testing. Agents cannot directly observe the spectrum, probe pins, or measure power, so they cannot verify wireless link functionality; currently, human engineers perform this verification. We systematically evaluate whether LLM agents can establish wireless links when provided

title: Agents' Last Doubt: Knowing When to Act and When to Step Back in Tool-Using Agents
authors: Qisai Liu, Qingyue Jiao, Bangwei Guo et al.
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents repeatedly face decision points under uncertainty, choosing between autonomous action, additional information gathering, and human escalation. These decisions require balancing task success against interaction cost and the risk of irreversible errors. Learning to make these trade-offs is challenging because existing interaction trajectories record only the outcomes of actions taken, leaving the consequences of alternative actions unobserved. title: Model Capacity Frontier: A Development Framework for LLM-Supported Social Simulation
authors: Patrick Zhao, Yuxuan Li, Hirokazu Shirado
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. title: Persistent Memory and Iterative Improvement in an LLM Agent for Chinese-Character Drawing
authors: Peilin Wu, Yi-Zhuang You
abstract: Does persistent memory accumulated from previous attempts help an LLM agent solve new problems, and does memory design affect that benefit? We study programmatic Chinese-character drawing across five agent conditions attempting the same 668 items. Accumulated memory produces modest aggregate gains despite substantial growth in the memory stores: free-form notes improve first-attempt success by 4.6 percentage points, while a design combining free-form memory with reusable code improves it by 2.8

title: OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners
authors: Peisong Wang, Feixue Liu, Yize Meng et al.
abstract: Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks typically begin with self-contained descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, underrepresenting the translation of original business materials into professionally validated solutions. title: The Window Is in the Reasoning: When LLM Agents Decide to Follow Prompt Injections
authors: Haoxuan Jia, Yang Liu, Bin Chong et al.
abstract: LLM agents that read untrusted content can be hijacked by prompt injections. Runtime monitors that try to catch a hijack before the agent acts, and benchmarks that score each task with a single run, share an assumption: whether an agent follows an injection is settled when the injection is read. title: LLM Evolution in a Simple Simulated Market
authors: Charlie Pilgrim, Christopher Krupenye, Dora Biro et al.
abstract: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces

title: CME-SpectrumBench: Can LLMs Analyze Condensed Matter Spectral Data?
authors: Jin Gene Wong, Anjney Midha, Joseph Mathew Tennyson et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are presently well assessed by expert-level mathematics and physics benchmarks which focus on theoretical, symbolic reasoning. However, we lack experimental benchmarks that evaluate data analysis in frontier research problems, a capability that future domain-specific foundation models must have. title: From SEC Filings to Financial Signals: Evaluating LLMs on Stock Market Reactions and Analyst Forecasts
authors: Shengkun Wang, Taoran Ji, Linhan Wang et al.
abstract: Form 10-Q MD&A sections combine long-form management narrative with accounting and forward-looking information. Benchmarks for financial filings commonly evaluate question answering or numerical reasoning, leaving unclear whether outputs from large language models (LLMs) align with market and analyst outcomes. We evaluate prompted, zero-shot outputs from 13 general-purpose and finance-specialized LLMs on 45,964 Form 10-Q filing events from 2001 to 2024, linking MD&A text to cross-section

title: Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay
authors: Wen-Zhi Li, Sainyam Galhotra, Claire Cardie
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. title: Multi-author style detection with stylistic embeddings
authors: Man-Ling Sung, Chak Fai Li, Damianos Karakos et al.
abstract: We investigate the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) in multi-author style change detection. Using off-the-shelf LLMs or supervised fine-tuning solely within the target domain fails to yield effective features; for this reason, we propose cross-domain transfer learning with LLM-based embeddings fine-tuned for authorship verification. title: Continual Test-Time Learning with Evolution Strategies
authors: Guangya Hao, Yiting Duan, Longyan Tan et al.
abstract: Large language models increasingly operate in open-ended environments, where they are expected to continually adapt to evolving tasks and distributions, often without access to external supervision. Existing continual learning approaches rely on external supervision, such as labeled data, demonstrations, or reward signals, which can be costly or unavailable in practice. title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Weight-Tied Transformers on Depth-Bound Algorithmic Tasks
authors: Magnus Sesodia, Juil Sock, Philip Torr et al.
abstract: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis
authors: Jian Yang, Peiling Liu, Songda Li et al.
abstract: Rare diseases (RDs) affect an estimated 300 million people globally, leaving patients to navigate a protracted diagnostic odyssey constrained by clinical scarcity and fragmented medical knowledge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively advanced RD diagnostics, from symbolic methods and deep learning to large language model (LLM)-based systems. title: Encoder-Free Multimodal LLMs Learn Implicit Encoders
authors: David Harwath, Desh Raj, Xavier Velez et al.
abstract: We empirically analyze two recently proposed encoder-free multimodal LLMs, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small. Unlike previous multimodal LLMs, these models do not use modality-specific encoders to extract tokenized embeddings representing audio and image input; instead, they directly feed windows of samples, pixels, or spectral features to the Transformer language model. title: Joint, Decoupled, or Agent: When Each Multimodal Alignment Paradigm Wins
authors: Yi Fang, Gaurav Srivastava, Sirui Ding et al.
abstract: Jointly pretrained multimodal encoders are a common way to combine modalities, while alternatives integrate their information during downstream training or inference. When does each approach win? We compare three paradigms, instantiated with public checkpoints, across 16 paired datasets in five domains and multiple training-label budgets. title: SLA-LENS: From Classroom Transcripts to CSLA-Informed and Evidence-Linked L2 Interaction Analytics
authors: Nemika Tyagi, Olga Kellert, Phanos Kareen et al.
abstract: What happens after a learner makes an error, and how does the instructor's response shape the next turn? Investigating these exchanges across classrooms requires context-sensitive annotation that is difficult to scale manually. We introduce SLA-LENS, an end-to-end LLM-assisted framework that connects classroom transcripts to structured pedagogical annotations and evidence-linked descriptive analytics. title: Cache2LoRA: Understanding and Improving Context Internalization
authors: Yi Fang, Gaurav Srivastava, Zhenyu Bi et al.
abstract: Context-to-LoRA methods encode documents as low-rank parameter updates, allowing language models to answer without retaining the source text in their decoding context. How reliably do these updates preserve facts and support their use under different instructions? Controlled diagnosis of existing context-to-LoRA methods separates fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation. title: BanglaShield: A Script-Robust Safety Classifier and Benchmark for Bangla Native, Romanized, and Code-Mixed Prompts
authors: Mohsinul Kabir, Md. Tariquzzaman, Mohammad Rashidujjaman Rifat et al.
abstract: Safety classifiers for large language models (LLMs) are typically built and evaluated on standard-script text, yet Bangla, like many lower-resource languages, is routinely written in native script, in Latin-script romanization, and code-mixed with English, Hindi, or Urdu. We introduce BanglaShield, a resource and model for graded prompt-safety classification across these written forms. title: SteerSearch: Interactive Search Reasoning with Mid-Response Steering
authors: Udit Thakur, Baohao Liao, Matteo Nulli et al.
abstract: Search-augmented language models increasingly serve as long-horizon research agents, yet most open training methods assume a fixed user goal throughout search. We study mid-response steering, where users redirect a model during ongoing reasoning or retrieval. We identify answer-target anchoring, a failure mode in which fixed-query search agents retrieve evidence for the updated request but still answer an earlier question. title: Language Models are Lazy Poets: Creative Mode Collapse at Scale
authors: Jacob A. Matthews, Sil Hamilton
abstract: While aligned large language models (LLMs) can successfully complete many creative tasks, their outputs tend to be highly self-similar. Though solutions to this problem of "mode collapse" have been proposed, comprehensive large-scale surveys of the phenomenon in specific textual genres are still lacking. We address this gap through an extensive treatment of LLM mode collapse in poetry. Across 15 poetic forms, 248 subject matter tags, and 16 open-weight models, we generate over 1.1 million poems.

title: Morpheus-2.0: Multiscale Probabilistic Forecasting with Dual-Axis Attention
authors: Aakriti, Manoj Cherukumalli, Prathamesh Patil et al.
abstract: A universal forecaster is trained once and applied everywhere, so it must serve tasks whose schemas, forecast horizons, and temporal resolutions all differ. The number of targets and covariates changes from dataset to dataset, horizons vary by orders of magnitude, and sampling rates range from seconds to years. title: An important Bottleneck in LLM Optimizers: Principle-Level Local Optima
authors: Nian Ran, Tianhe Jia, Zhengyang Mu et al.
abstract: Feedback-driven LLM optimizers are increasingly used for evolutionary search, Bayesian optimization, heuristic design, and scientific discovery. Yet rapid initial gains often give way to prolonged plateaus despite substantial remaining evaluation budgets. We investigate \emph{principle-level search collapse}, where an optimizer's search becomes confined to a narrow set of design principles, even though it may continue to generate distinct candidates and achieve small improvements. title: SPIDES: Information-Flow Control for Browser Agents
authors: Egor Zverev, Juhee Kim, Leon Trampert et al.
abstract: Browser agents automate complex workflows by reading and acting on arbitrary page content, but this flexibility exposes them to prompt injection attacks and unintended data exfiltration. Recent work argues that LLM-driven browser agents erode traditional web security boundaries such as the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) by acting across origins with the user's authority and no built-in isolation. title: Prefix-Tuning for Arbitrary Output Sequences on Pretrained Transformers
authors: Peter Cho-Ho Lam, Ziyi Wang, Zirui Zhou
abstract: Prefix-tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models (LLMs) that steers model outputs by prepending task-specific prefix representations to the input sequence. Despite its practical success, the theoretical understanding of the expressiveness of prefixes remains incomplete. title: IRAH: Hierarchical Agentic Tree Search for Retrieval Pipeline Optimization
authors: Maria Ana Cardei, Aniket Singh, Amir Moghadam et al.
abstract: Optimizing Information Retrieval (IR) pipelines for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) requires jointly selecting structural components and numerical hyperparameters under limited evaluation budgets. We introduce the Information Retrieval Agentic Harness (IRAH), which combines Language Agent Tree Search for IR (LATS-IR) with offline meta-learned initialization. title: Private Retrieval Augmented Generation via Random Projection
authors: Dixi Yao, Tahseen Rabbani, Tian Li
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by querying external structured knowledge. However, it can also introduce privacy risks by leaking sensitive information from the retrieval datastore. We propose a simple method to preserve datastore privacy in RAG systems via random projection. title: Multi-sourced AI Tutor for Non-Native English Speaker Students
authors: Yiyin Shen, Xinyi Ai, Weibing Wang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted as teaching tools in computing education, particularly for developing AI tutors capable of answering student questions. With the rise in enrollment of international students in computing programs, researchers have begun to explore the difficulties that non-native English speaker (NNES) students face in computing courses due to language barriers. title: RAG-RST: Retrieved Exemplars as In-Context Discourse Schema for RST Parsing
authors: Mohammadreza Sediqin, Shlomo Engelson Argamon
abstract: In Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST), each edge of a discourse tree carries a nuclearity label, marking which span holds the central content, and a relation drawn from a closed inventory of functional categories. title: CARA: Causally Guided Retrieval Agent for Question Answering
authors: Weicheng Liu, Xiangcheng Wu, Depeng Xu et al.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over text-rich knowledge graphs requires identifying evidence that contributes to answering a question, rather than merely matching its textual content. Existing agentic retrievers adaptively balance global search and multi-hop exploration but primarily rely on textual similarity to guide retrieval. title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents
authors: Pengfeng Song, Yunkai Zhuang, Liye Shi
abstract: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. title: Loud and Clear: Making Visual Evidence Count in Multimodal Document RAG
authors: Eunchan Jo, Seounghyun Jang, Sangwoo Mo
abstract: Multimodal document retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has focused largely on retrieval, yet its answers depend on how well a vision-language model reads the retrieved pages. We find that evidence in retrieved pages remains underused even when the correct pages are retrieved. title: Beyond Retrieval Failure: Understanding Why LLMs Miss Evidence in Multi-Hop RAG
authors: Jiaqi Wei, Wenxuan Huang, Chengdong Xu et al.
abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires an agent to retrieve evidence for a sequence of dependent sub-questions. When a wrong answer lacks a required passage, the passage may be inaccessible to the retriever, or the agent may have failed to issue a query that would retrieve it. title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
authors: Shangheng Du, Jinxin Shi, Shuaiyu Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). title: Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Leyang Shen, Yaxin Gong, Yang Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
authors: Anikait Singh, Teresa Zhang, Yoonho Lee et al.
abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. title: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning
authors: Bingxiang He, Pengqi Sun, Shihao Peng et al.
abstract: Language model agents increasingly automate post-training, but when given the full training stack they converge on supervised fine-tuning and spend most effort revising training data. Existing systems give the agent one kind of control, selecting rows from a fixed pool or calling a generator, whereas a human data engineer adjusts proportions, prunes, repairs, replaces and synthesizes the data. title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
authors: Kshitij Mishra, Abhijith Sharma, Nils Lukas et al.
abstract: Modern agentic systems extend language models with external tools, enabling them to complete complex tasks through multi-turn interactions. As these agents are deployed in consequential settings, they are often constrained by policies governing pricing, privacy, confirmation, safety, and other requirements. title: GraphACM: Graph-based Action Consistency Measurement for Uncertainty Quantification in LLM Agents
authors: Yaxin Ma, Wenbo Zhang, Satya Krishna Pothapragada et al.
abstract: Behavioral consistency across repeated executions provides an informative signal for assessing the reliability of large language model (LLM) agents. However, existing approaches typically summarize consistency with a single task-level score, without identifying where behavioral differences occur or whether actions are compared under equivalent decision contexts. title: OntoAct: Hypothesis-Based Neuro-Symbolic Agents through Ontological Abstraction
authors: Donghyeok Lee, Bong Gyun Kang, Junyong Ahn et al.
abstract: Learning from experience requires recovering reusable knowledge and determining when it applies to a new situation. We introduce OntoAct, a hypothesis-based neuro-symbolic framework built on ontological abstraction. OntoAct turns individual experiences into axioms over entity types, relations, and conditions, making their underlying patterns reusable across situations. title: Agentic-Priors: Using Large Language Models to Address the Cold Start Problem in Preference Elicitation
authors: Bruno Arcanjo, Zhaoxing Li, Sebastian Stein
abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
authors: Lo Gullstrand Heander, Markus Borg, Emma Söderberg et al.
abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. authors: Huan Zhang, Mingju Chen, Dongxu Zhou et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. title: DeciCAD: Harness-Grounded Learning of Action Policies for CAD Agents
authors: Yufeng Peng, Yixin Zhang, Ziyi Liu et al.
abstract: Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness. We investigate how this operating space shapes agent behavior and policy learning in computer-aided design (CAD), a professional domain characterized by persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures. title: The Delegation Dilemma: Economies of Scale, Accountability, and Polycentric Governance
authors: Arin Mukhopadhyay, Aris Filos-Ratsikas, Panayiotis Danassis
abstract: Many collective-action systems are neither fully decentralized nor fully centralized: agents voluntarily organize into institutions that share organizational costs and delegate decisions to representatives. Delegation can reduce individual costs, but it also transfers control to representatives whose private objectives need not align with those of their constituents. title: Human Interventions as Labels: Localizing, Steering, and (Sometimes) Editing the Computations Behind LLM Agent Failures
authors: Cesare Zavattari, Alessandro Tommasi, Giuseppe Prencipe
abstract: When an LLM agent misbehaves, a human steps in, and that intervention is usually discarded or replayed as training data. We treat it instead as a measurement: a label pointing at the internal computation that failed. title: The Self-Improvement Problem
authors: Brian B. Moser, Stanislav Frolov, Tobias C. Nauen et al.
abstract: With the rise of large language models, agentic systems are becoming increasingly autonomous, as they write code, call tools, revise prompts, and propose modifications to their own components. title: AgentPerturb: Evaluating LLM Agent Robustness under Controlled Interaction Perturbations
authors: Yuanjian Xu, Jinyi Han, Jianing Hao et al.
abstract: Real-world tasks are often complex and noisy, posing substantial challenges for LLM agents. Yet existing evaluations lack a systematic framework for jointly characterizing potential perturbation targets and types. title: Evaluating Inquiry Learning in LLM-Based Agents: Hypothesizing, Reasoning, and Exploration
authors: Marta Knežević, Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Jibril Frej et al.
abstract: Scientific inquiry involves iterative cycles of exploration, hypothesis generation, and reasoning over observations to uncover relationships in complex systems. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in several components of this process, including inductive reasoning, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. title: Rethinking the Role of Tool Graph Memory in Multi-Turn Tool Use
authors: Uiji Hwang, Richeng Xuan, Taeuk Kim
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents' tool use or undermines it. title: Independent Data-Integrity Verification for LLM-Driven Functional Coverage Closure in Hardware Design
authors: Venkata Krishna Kumar Vedantam
abstract: LLM agents can write directed tests that close functional coverage, but coverage only shows that a state was reached, not that the data on the way there was correct. This is a long-known point in verification and we do not claim it as new. authors: Sergio Burdisso, Esaú Villatoro-Tello, Dairazalia Sánchez-Cortés et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. title: ISW-Agent: Integrating LLM-Driven Dialogue with n8n Workflow for Internal Solitary Wave Remote Sensing Image Processing
authors: Hao Zhang, Hengrui Liu, Lina Sun et al.
abstract: Internal solitary wave (ISW) remote sensing requires task parameters and spatial information to be transferred across image acquisition, detection, stripe extraction, and propagation prediction. Here, we present ISW-Agent, which integrates large language model (LLM) interpretation with n8n workflows and independent scientific models through structured task constraints, geospatial transformations, and stage-specific output validation. title: MetaExp: Learning to Self-Improve through Experience via Verifiable Cross-Task Environment Scaling
authors: Renhao Li, Xinjie Shen, Yang Su et al.
abstract: Language-model agents can accumulate interaction feedback, but reliably turning that feedback into reusable experience remains challenging. Existing methods either optimize external experience scaffolds or train experience-related behavior on specific task distributions, leaving open whether experience learning itself can become a transferable model capability. authors: Zilin Wang, Yinhong Liu, Chao Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. authors: Kunlun Zhu, Tao Feng, Xu Han et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. authors: Cheng Zhang, Xuanning Cao, Zhicheng Zheng et al.
abstract: Long-term memory has become a crucial component of large language model (LLM) agents, with most research focusing on retrieving relevant information accurately and efficiently. However, a dependable memory system must also forget sensitive user data upon request. To evaluate this capability, we introduce MemCut, a systematic benchmark for user-requested forgetting. title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Han Shen, Qifu Tyler Sun, Fanyang Meng et al.
abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. authors: Boxun Lan, Jiamei Li, Weijian Li et al.
abstract: Large language model agents can improve their capabilities by evolving reusable natural-language skills from execution experience. In real-world deployments, this experience is distributed across data owners who cannot pool their raw data, which motivates federated skill evolution. authors: Junru Wu, Jingting Zheng, Yuqi Ren et al.
abstract: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. title: Bias Control and Injection for Multi-Agent Aggregation
authors: Sungjae Lee, Soheil Abbasloo, Jabin Koo et al.
abstract: Multi-agent reasoning with large language models (LLMs) raises a central question for collective decision-making: when agents disagree, whose decision should be trusted? Resolving such disagreements is difficult because agents' decisions are susceptible to non-semantic biases such as majority pressure and response-style preferences, which can obscure the quality of the underlying reasoning. title: Diviner: Agentic RCA with Human-Governed Adaptation for Large-Scale Infrastructure
authors: Pradipta Ghosh, Gaurav Mitra, Shripad Nadgowda et al.
abstract: Root-cause analysis (RCA) in large-scale distributed systems is challenging because a single symptom can cross service, data, configuration, compute, and organizational boundaries. Responders must assemble incomplete evidence and coordinate experts who hold different parts of the causal path. authors: Zihao Zheng, Junyi Yao, Baichuan Li et al.
abstract: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. authors: Tanish Kher, Sarvesh DK, Abedelkadir Asi et al.
abstract: Modern agents select tools from registries, but exposing entire registries incurs high token costs and can impair selection as they grow. We present TRACER, a retrieval front-end that indexes observed tool-call sequences in a trie and ranks continuations using a learned blend of empirical and contextual priors. authors: Zane Durante, Paul Tang, Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran et al.
abstract: Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. authors: Tanay Arora, Cong Liu
abstract: Agentic large language models have been documented to lose reasoning capability when placed inside a harness, the software that mediates their observations and actions. To reconcile these losses, we introduce AutoOnboarder, an autonomous system that adapts an agent to a task the way a trainer onboards a new employee. authors: Miao Su, Yucan Guo, Zixuan Li et al.
abstract: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. authors: Bingbing Wang, Jingjie Lin, Weiming Qiao et al.
abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long-horizon histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents. authors: Jianchang Su, Dawei Xiang, Yifan Zhang et al.
abstract: LLM-agent evaluation reports behavioral scores but leaves the identity of the deployed runtime stack unreported. A tampered deployment that preserves evaluated outputs passes every output-only evaluator. authors: Giancarlo Maldonado Cárdenas, Carlos A. Astudillo, Nelson L. S. da Fonseca
abstract: Large-scale multi-agent ecosystems require mechanisms for discovering suitable agents without exposing entire registries to a large language model (LLM) orchestrator. authors: Yixuan Xie, Xueqiang Xu, Xinyi Fan et al.
abstract: Agent memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experiences without updating their parameters. However, semantic similarity alone does not guarantee memory usefulness: downstream performance depends on how memories are selected and presented to the agent. authors: Youran Sun, Xingyu Ren, Chugang Yi et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. authors: Zhaoqian Xue, Shaoze Zhou, Xuexin Li et al.
abstract: Systematic literature reviews follow the PRISMA process of screening scholarly works and extracting evidence from included studies. Deep research tools based on large language models (LLMs) can search and summarize the literature but do not record which studies are excluded or where extracted values come from. authors: Sai Varun Kodathala, Prashanth Pollishetty, Jaylen Cargill
abstract: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. authors: Alexey A. Bokov, Ivan I. Panin, Nikolay B. Nechaev et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate differential diagnoses for complex cases, but a useful second opinion must also be factually grounded, clinically coherent, actionable, and safe. authors: Wei Cai, Jian Zhao, Yuchen Yuan et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can act unsafely when individually benign images and texts are interpreted jointly. authors: Daniel Palacios, Guantong Qi, Mikael Guzman Karlsson et al.
abstract: Objective: Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. authors: Shuoran Jiang, Wentao Zhu, Yang Xiang et al.
abstract: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity.
